newsitem.title: PERU: Peru police blast night music at Marxist rebels.
newsitem.headline: Peru police blast night music at Marxist rebels.

text.p: Peru blasted martial music in the early hours on Thursday at Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home as part of stepped-up police efforts to weaken the guerrillas' resolve in the 44-day siege.

The military tunes blaring from three loudspeakers placed around the residence shattered the night's silence around the capital's middle-class district of San Isidro just after 1 a.m. EST (0600 GMT). The noise woke neighbours, who came to their windows and doorsteps and stared dazed at the speakers.
"It's really loud. Nobody could sleep with this racket," said Reuters photographer Manuel Llanos at the site.
The soundtrack played for about half an hour and included the noise of aircraft, creating the impression helicopters and planes approaching the fortified compound, witnesses said.
After the music a police armoured vehicle rumbled several times around the residence at a distance of one block.

Police have played the music periodically for several days to wear down the roughly 15 heavily armed Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement rebels inside the mined and booby- trapped compound. Thursday was the first time the police turned on the music during sleeping hours.
The music was part of heightened police activity at the site this week.

Scores of police took part in a massive show of force in front of the compound on Monday, driving past in an armoured convoy to the tune of the marching music. Some made obscene gestures, provoking a burst a gunfire from the rebels which narrowly missed policemen aboard one vehicle.

Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto called earlier this week for Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori to exercise caution in the deployment of police at the site to prevent "accidents or incidents."
The two leaders agreed Wednesday to an urgent meeting this weekend in Canada to try to discuss the deadlocked crisis.
Calling for the meeting in Toronto at 10 a.m. (1500 GMT) Saturday was a sign of growing concern in Lima and Tokyo that the crisis could drag on and endanger the hostages' lives.
"President Fujimori has told us he wants to discuss the Peruvian situation with me as soon as possible," Hashimoto told reporters in Japan.

"I can't go into details at this delicate stage but what we must confirm is that we must not cave in to terrorism and at the same time seek the release of all captives unharmed and as soon as possible," he told a parliamentary committee later.

On Thursday Hashimoto said there would be no "caving in to terrorism" in solving the crisis, but officials said Hashimoto was likely to temper the tough talk with a plea that Lima avoid steps that could prompt the rebels to harm the hostages.
About two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats, including Ambassador Morihisa Aoki, were being held captive by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels.

"In the planned meeting, aspects of the strategy set out to reach a solution to the takeover of the residence will be evaluated jointly," Peru's chief crisis negotiator Domingo Palermo told a news conference.

A senior government official told Reuters: "He (Fujimori) will not meet with Hashimoto to apologise for the police attitude nor is he going to Canada to ask permission (from Japan) to enter the residence (by force)."
The official, who requested anonymity, added that Fujimori would travel to Washington after the Toronto meeting "to thank U.S. President Bill Clinton for his support."
Canada would host the talks because of its mediating role in the crisis which has been accepted by both sides, Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien said.
Efforts to start talks with the MRTA guerrillas have stalled over the main rebel demand of freedom for about 400 jailed comrades, which Fujimori has refused to discuss.
The MRTA rebels originally seized hundreds of guests when they stormed a garden party at the residence Dec. 17.
They released most of the captives but kept those they consider the most important bargaining chips.
